2 Verbs
French verbs are divided into three groups, depending on the end
ing of the infinitive. (Unlike English infinitives, which are formed
with to, French infinitives consist of a single word). By far the
largest group comprises verbs ending in -er. We have already seen
quite a few of them, including appeler, to calf, chercher, to look for,
désirer, to want, penser, to think, présenter, to introduce, tourner,
to turn, and traverser, to cross.
As in English, French verb endings change depending on the 'per
san' doing the action (think, but she thinks). Let's see what we have
learned already:
je pense, / think, vous pensez,you [formai] think, and nous pen
sons, we think.
As you can see, there are more forms than in English, which gen
erally has just two in the present tense, but you will soon get the
hang of them. Remember, too, that there are no continuous verb
forms in French, so je cherche means both / look for and / am
looking for.

• The months of the year are:

None of the day or month nouns take an initial capital (unless they

When giving the date, French uses a cardinal number, not an ordi

month, as in English:

This sub-category, comprising irregular verbs such as sortir, ta go

the irregular dormir is dormant.

go.

Present participles, seen in tesson 22 note 9 and tesson 23 note 6,
are used less than in English because there is no progressive verb

the participle is formed by dropping the ending from the first per

penser ➔ pensons ➔ pensant;

The negative is formed by placing ne ... pas around the auxiliary:

The three forms of the interrogative are (i) a rising tone Tu as vu ?
(ii) with est-ce que: Est-ce que tu as vu? or (iii) inversion: As-tu vu?
The perfect tense relates to actions that took place in the past and
are now complete. ln this context, it is equivalent to the past simple
tense in English: ]'ai vu le notaire hier, / saw the notary yesterday.
But if we remove the time marker hier, the French verb remains
the same (J'ai vu le notaire), whereas the English equivalent is
either / saw or the present perfect, / have seen the notary.
When adverbs such as jamais and toujours are used with le passé
composé, the verb is translated with the present perfect:
J'ai toujours voulu / Je n'ai jamais voulu apprendre le français.

ln some cases, however, particularly with the preposition depuis,
which translates bothfor and since, French uses the present rather
than a perfect tense:

3 Comparatives and superlatives
• The comparative of superiority is always formed with plus before
the adjective and que aer it:
Londres est plus grand que Paris., London is bigger than Paris.
Unlike English, the length of the adjective does not matter:
Paris est plus cher que Bruxelles.
Paris is more expensive than Brussets.
• The same rule applies to comparisons of inferiority, formed with
moins ... que:
Le film est moins intéressant que le livre.
The movie is tess interesting than the book.
(ln some cases, particularly moins cher, English can choose
between the superior or the inferior comparative: it's cheaper I
less expensive .)
• To form the superlative, simply put the definite article le or la
for the singular (masculine/feminine) and les for the plural before
plus or moins:
Le bus est le moyen le plus rapide d'aller à Lille.
The bus is the quickest way to get to Lille;

lt's the teast noisy district in the city.

4 On the phone
Using the telephone can be difficult, even in one's native lan
guage, for many reasons. ln a foreign language, those difficulties
are compounded by rapid speech, an unfamiliar vocabulary and,
usually, being unable to see the persan you are talking to. And
although texting, videoconferencing and other forms of digital
communication are omni-present, being able to communicate by
phone -téléphone (portable) (mobile) or fixe (landline)-is still an
important skill to learn. (lnterestingly, although most communica
tions today are wireless, the familiar expression for a phone cal/ is
still un coup de fil!)
Here are some of the set phrases used in most conversations.
• Allô is used when answering the phone or checking that the
persan you are calling can hear you. (One variant is Allô oui ?,
although some people reply simply Oui ?, which is just as abrupt
as Yes? in English.) To enquire about the identity of the calier, use
the expression Qui est à l'appareil ? Who is calling ? (see tesson 31) .
• To confirm that you have reached the right number, say Je suis
bien chez ... ? (for a persan) or Je suis bien au/à la ... (for a busi
ness, an administration, etc.)
• If you ask to speak to someone other than the persan answer
ing, you will usually be asked: C'est de la part de qui ? (or, more
succinctly and less politely, De la part de qui ?) Who sha/1 I say is
calling?

1.1 Formation
The passive voice of a verb is formed with être and the past participle.
Les gens l'aiment, People love him ➔ Il est aimé, He's /oved.
ln the past tense, être becomes été and the two participles follow
each other:
Ils ont fermé le pont hier, They c/osed the bridge yesterday
➔ Le pont a été fermé hier, The bridge was c/osed yesterday.
ln these two examples, the passive is used because the fact of being
loved or closed is more important than whoever is doing the loving
or closing.

One slight difference with the English construction is that the past
participle, being an adjective, has to agree with the subject of the
passive verb: Ils ont fermé la fenêtre ➔ La fenêtre a été fermée.
(Now's the time to revise your past participles!)
If the active subject is incorporated as an agent into the passive
sentence, it is preceded by par, by:
Le maire a fermé le pont, The mayor closed the bridge
➔ Le pont a été fermé par le maire, The bridge was closed by the
mayor.
Of course, the participle agreement rule does not change (L'école
a été fermée par le maire). Where the agent is mentioned, par is
used for almost ail verbs. However, those expressing a feeling or an
emotion (aimer, respecter, admirer) or a state (entourer, couvrir,
décorer, etc.) tend to use de rather than par:
Le metteur en scène est respecté de tout le monde.
The director is respected by everybody.
There are only a handful of such verbs, so they are easy to learn.
The negative and first and second interrogatives follow the usual
rules:
Le pont n'a pas été fermé; Est-ce que le pont a été fermé ?
The third interrogative is slightly more complicated -Le pont a-t
il été fermé ? -but is used much less than the other two forms.
1.2 Use
The passive is used less in French than in English, firstly because
active forms are preferable when describing actions, and secondly
because French has several ways of sidestepping passive con
structions. There are three main workarounds: with on, with the
pronominal form, and with c'est ... qui.
• with on:
The third-person impersonal pronoun on is used when the subject
is implied or unimportant. lt replaces nous, ils/elles, quelqu'un,
tout le monde, etc. So a sentence like Ici, on parle anglais can be
used by a shop to inform potential customers that ail its staff speak
English (We speak English here), or by residents of an area to insist
447 • quatre cent quarante-sept

that everyone is anglophone (Everyone here speaks Engtish). As you
know, on is also commonly used instead of nous, simply because
the first-person plural verb form oen sounds tao formai. ln very
formai situations, on can be translated by its English cognate, one.
For example, On dit que ... can be the equivalent of One says that .. .
but it would generally be rendered by the passive It is said that .. .
ln a more colloquial setting, the usual equivalent is They say that .. .
• with the pronominal verbs, formed with se:
These are more common in French than in English precisely because
they are used instead of the passive voice. ln this case, there is no
notion of myse/J, itse/J, etc. For example: Ce plat se mange chaud
ou froid means This dish is eaten hot or cold. This form is possible
only with the third persan singular or plural: Les voitures neuves se
vendent bien cette année, New cars are selling wett this year. One
very common set of short passive phrases is formed with ça (or, more
formally, cela) followed by a pronominal verb: Il est français. - Ça
s'entend, He's French. - You can hear it. Elle a très mal. - Cela se
voit, She's in great pain. -That's obvious, etc.
• with c'est (plural: ce sont) ... qui:
This workaround avoids the passive by emphasising the subject. So
a sentence like The report was written by my Çerman colleague can
be translated literally by Le rapport a été écrit par mon collègue
allemand, which is grammatically correct, or, more colloquially,
by C'est mon collègue allemand qui a écrit le rapport. A word
for-word translation ("lt's my Çerman colleague who ... ," etc) does
not have the same resonance, precisely because French prefers the
active to the passive.
The main difference between the two languages is that the passive
cannot be used with an indirect abject in French, unlike English.

4 Adjectives of dimension
Dimensions can be expressed in several ways. The adjectives
long(ue), haut(e), large and profond(e) are placed before the noun,

Maxims are an integral part any language and are used regularly,
either directly or obliquely ("Vou know what they say about rolling
stones ..." ). ln any case, they are an important part of popular cul
ture. Because French and English are closely related, many proverbs

blames his tools;

1 Le subjonctif: the subjunctive
The subjunctive mood describes a hypothetical situation. lt is gen
erally used in a subordinate clause to talk about actions or events
that are desirable, imagined or possible, and that generally depend
on an initial verb in the indicative.
The subjunctive exists in English but, being almost identical to the
indicative, is rarely identified as such (except in phrases such as /
wish I were on holiday). ln French, however, it is bath common and
obligatory. This is especially the case in subordinate clauses where
the subject is different from the one in the main clause and where
the action being described is in some way conditional, theoretical
or subjective. ln this case, the subordinate verb is preceded by que.
For example, Je veux que tu sois heureuse, / wantyou to be happy
(i.e. the persan l'm talking to seems miserable -my subjective opin
ion-and I wish they weren't).
There are four subjunctive tenses (present, past, imperfect and
pluperfect) but in modern, conversational French, we generally use
the present form (and occasionally the past).
1.1 Formation
The present subjunctive is formed by taking the third persan plural
of the present tense, dropping the final -ent and adding the end
ings shown below.
aimer finir attendre
j'aime je finisse j'attende
tu aimes tu finisse tu attendes

The simple way to negate a verb is with ne ... pas (Il comprend➔ Il
ne comprend pas). But there are other constructions in which pas

Ils ne veulent jamais venir en vacances avec nous.

• ne ... plus, no longer, no more,

becomes de:

Whereas est-ce que is the most common interrogative construction

1.2 Use
The passé simple is used to describe a completed, discrete action
in the past that has no link to or is uni mportant in the present:
Elle fut choisie par le roi, qui l'épousa.
She was chosen by the king, who married here.
Toute la Cour fit un grand banquet.
The entire court held a huge banquet.
Le roi et sa reine eurent quatre enfants ensemble.
The king and his queen had four children together.
But despite the "historie" tag, the tense is not confined to history
books. Here's a passage from a much-loved novel, Le Petit Prince
"The Little Prince''. by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry:
li n'y eut rien qu'un éclair jaune près de sa cheville. li demeura
un instant immobile. li ne cria pas. li tomba doucement comme
tombe un arbre. Ça ne fit même pas de bruit, à cause du sable.
There was nothing but a yellow flash near his ankle. He remained
motionless for a moment. He did not scream. He Je// softly, as a tree
fa lis. lt did not even make any noise, because of the sand.)
Nowadays, most young French speakers learn only the third per
sans singular and plural; and most contemporary authors narrate
using le passé composé and le présent historique (lesson 42 note
2), prompting some grammarians to predict the imminent demise
of le passé simple. Even so, a basic knowledge of how to conjugate
the main verbs in this case is important.
1.3 Differences with English
Ali the actions described with le passé simple are completed,
whereas repeated actions in the past require the imperfect. ln
English, though, we can use the past simple in both cases. Compare:
li m'envoyait des lettres tous les jours pendant son voyage.
He sent me letters every day white he was travelling.
With:
li m'envoya une lettre le premier jour de son voyage, et une
autre à son retour.
